messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla is a 43-year-old Iranian-American pharmacist, married and living in a mid-sized Midwestern city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to her primary care physician of self-harming behaviour. Her PCL-5 score of 71 places her presentation in the severe range, and the clinical picture that has emerged across intake and early sessions is one of a woman whose childhood has never, in any meaningful sense, ended.

Layla grew up in a household where her father's drinking was the weather system around which every other life event organised itself. The smell of alcohol on his breath was the first signal — before the shouting, before the commands, before the blows — that the evening was about to turn. He was a man who issued orders with the certainty of someone who expected absolute compliance, and non-compliance was punished physically and without hesitation. Layla learned early to read the room, to stay alert, to anticipate. She carried that vigilance with her when she emigrated as a young adult, and she carries it still.

She has worked as a pharmacist for fourteen years, and it is in the dispensary that her symptoms press most concretely against her daily life. When a supervising physician phones in a correction with a clipped, authoritative tone, or when a hospital administrator walks through the pharmacy floor, Layla's body responds before her mind can intervene — her chest tightens, her attention scatters, and she finds herself scanning for threat in a room where none exists. These false alarms are exhausting and disorienting, and they bleed directly into her difficulty concentrating during medication checks, a lapse that frightens her professionally. The workplace itself has become a minefield: the antiseptic smell occasionally mingles with something that catches at the back of her throat and pulls her backward, and on two occasions a colleague's cologne, carrying faint notes of ethanol, was enough to send her into the corridor. Each time a trigger fired — each time the smell or the tone of voice landed — it arrived with a thought she could not argue away: that she was helpless, that she had always been helpless, that no amount of professional competence or careful living had ever changed that fact. Being given instructions by anyone in a position of authority — a routine feature of her working day — now reliably activates the same alarm system her childhood built, and in the wake of those moments she has begun quietly engineering her schedule to minimise contact with senior staff. Already running on threat, she found that the very strategies she had adopted to reduce her exposure had paradoxically sharpened her sensitivity — the rerouted schedule, the avoided corridors, the carefully managed silences had drawn a map of danger around her, so that each detour was its own daily reminder, and the world she moved through had grown smaller and more charged.

When triggers fire, the memories do not arrive as recollections so much as intrusions. Layla describes them as more real than anything happening in front of her — her father's face, the specific quality of the kitchen light, the sound of a belt — and when they return with full force she is overwhelmed so rapidly by emotion that she has to stop whatever she is doing and find somewhere private. After the memory had surfaced and receded, she would find herself moving through the rest of the day with every sense sharpened to the wrong frequency — a door closing too firmly, a male colleague's raised voice two aisles over, the particular weight of silence before someone spoke — each one now threaded through with the logic of the memory, readable as warning. At other times, and she finds this equally disturbing, she can narrate the same events in a flat, dissociated voice, as though they happened to someone she read about. The memories themselves feed the threat system: having been flooded once, she cannot fall asleep without monitoring the sounds of the house, certain on some level that danger is still circulating. That hypervigilance, in turn, keeps the memories closer to the surface, and the surface closer to the past. Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the background hum of threat she carried everywhere had quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, that this was simply who she was now.

What Layla has come to believe about herself is, in many ways, the most entrenched part of her presentation. She is certain that she cannot prevent bad things from happening to her — that she never could — and this conviction of helplessness colours everything. The belief that she was permanently damaged kept returning her to the memories themselves, as though her mind needed to locate the exact moment the damage had been done — the memories sat there waiting, proof of a verdict she had already accepted. She has failed, she believes, in her most important role: she is not the mother she should be, not the wife she intended to be, and the meaning she once found in her work has drained away. These appraisals do not stay abstract. Once she had accepted the conclusion that she was fundamentally incapable of safety, almost anything could confirm it — a clipped instruction, a shadow in her peripheral vision, the particular silence of a room before someone entered — things she might once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her, the world suddenly dense with signals she felt compelled to read. When she begins to feel hopeful — when a family dinner goes well, when she receives praise at work — she withdraws from the feeling, as though allowing it would be a kind of hubris that invites punishment. Her avoidance of positive emotional states has become systematic, a habit that has quietly narrowed her life and bewildered her husband. And when the appraisals are loudest, when the sense of helplessness is most suffocating, she hurts herself — a controlled pain that interrupts the unbearable mental noise, that gives her something she can, briefly, manage. But the relief was always temporary: she had been suppressing and sidestepping the material for so long, keeping it at arm's length through avoidance and the brief interruption of self-harm, that when the memories returned they were louder than before — undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left them, all that effort of containment having kept them perfectly preserved. She knows this is not a solution. It was the shame of this, finally, that brought her to her doctor's office: not the fear of the memories, but the fear of what she is becoming, and a faint, carefully guarded hope that something might still be different. Feeling this afraid all the time had eventually produced its own conclusion — that she was not the mother she should have been, not the wife she had intended to be, that the life she had tried to build was simply further proof of a helplessness that had always been hers.
